analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer loan interest at 36% APR and bans payday lending nationwide.
analysis.headline: The FAIR Act, a 36% interest-rate cap and payday lending ban, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in September 2008 and died there with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for any lender other than a bank or credit union to charge more than 36% annual interest on a consumer loan, with all fees counted toward that rate. It would have banned payday lending practices like cashing post-dated checks for fees and holding a borrower's car title or bank account access as loan collateral. Loans made in violation would have been void, with lenders forced to return all principal, interest, and fees. To replace the lost credit, it would have directed the FDIC to create a voluntary program encouraging banks to offer small loans of $1,000 or less on affordable terms.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers with low incomes and limited access to mainstream credit, who currently turn to payday, auto-title, and high-rate installment lenders when they need cash. A 36% cap with all fees included would have ended the loan structures that routinely push such borrowers into effective triple-digit rates and repeated rollovers, and voided loans would have let consumers erase the debt and reclaim collateral. It also would have leaned on banks and credit unions — which were exempted from the cap — to fill the gap with small-dollar loan products that count toward their Community Reinvestment Act obligations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income borrowers using payday and high-cost lenders

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any consumer loan from a non-bank creditor at 36%, with all fees, credit insurance premiums, and ancillary charges counted into that rate, so lenders cannot disguise the true cost [S3].
Bans payday lending mechanics: cashing or advancing money on post-dated checks for a fee, and holding a check, electronic account access, or a vehicle title as loan collateral [S3].

Makes any loan made in violation null and void, requires the lender to return all principal, interest, and fees, and lets consumers raise the violation as a defense at any time, with criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and fines up to three times the debt or $50,000 per violation [S3].

Directs the FDIC to establish a voluntary program for insured banks to offer small loans of $1,000 or less with amortization of up to 36 months, no prepayment penalties, and no fees beyond the true cost of the loan, and counts participation under the Community Reinvestment Act [S2].
Lets state attorneys general enforce the rate cap in federal court within three years of a violation, adding an enforcement backstop beyond individual lawsuits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday, auto-title, and high-rate installment lenders would lose the core of their business model, since a 36% all-in rate cap with voided loans and criminal penalties makes triple-digit-rate lending unprofitable and legally risky. Some consumers who relied on those loans would have had fewer options in the short run unless banks and credit unions expanded small-dollar lending under the FDIC program; the bill's own small-dollar loan and study provisions exist to address that gap.

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% cap can cut off credit entirely for borrowers whose risk profile lenders judge unprofitable to serve at that rate. The bill tries to handle this by exempting banks and credit unions and pushing an FDIC small-dollar loan program, but whether mainstream institutions would lend at scale to the same customers, on reasonable terms, was unproven [S3].

Voiding entire loans and returning all principal and fees, rather than just the excess charges, raises the risk that some borrowers would lose access to credit altogether and that lenders would stop serving marginal borrowers, a trade-off an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill targets, the upside is large: ending loan structures that routinely produce effective triple-digit annual rates and debt traps. The main cost is that some borrowers with poor credit could have lost access to short-term cash unless the bank and credit union small-dollar program scaled up to replace it. That replacement mechanism was a real but untested part of the design, and it is the strongest good-faith objection to the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late September 2008 and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the FAIR Act on September 26, 2008, in the final weeks of a Congress in its final months [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point [S4].

The bill's core provisions would have capped consumer loan APR at 36%, banned payday lending mechanics, voided violating loans, and created an FDIC program to encourage banks to offer affordable small-dollar loans [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, auto-title, and other high-cost consumer lenders are better off, because the bill died without a vote and their business models survived untouched. Borrowers continued paying whatever rates state law allowed.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the FAIR Act and introduced it in the Senate on September 26, 2008.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever held.

against.name: Payday and consumer lending industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have capped rates at 36% and voided loans, ending the industry's core lending model; industry opposition to federal rate caps is well documented.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to reveal a partisan split: one Democratic senator sponsored it, it drew no cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a vote [S4].

industries.note: A 36% all-in APR cap plus a ban on holding post-dated checks, account access, or car titles as collateral would have eliminated the industry's core products, and voided-loan provisions plus criminal penalties would have made past-model lending unenforceable. These lenders profit from fees that translate to triple-digit annual rates charged to financially stretched borrowers.

industries.industry: Subprime installment and consumer finance companies
industries.note: Non-bank consumer lenders above the rate cap would have faced the same 36% limit, mandatory disclosures, and voided-loan liability, including on credit insurance and ancillary product charges that currently add to borrower costs.

Insured depository institutions and credit unions are exempted from the rate cap, and the bill directs the FDIC to run a voluntary small-dollar loan program with credit toward Community Reinvestment Act obligations for participating — creating a potential new lending market on favorable terms.
